text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Diagnosis: blood count with MCV, smear and reticulocytes; vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine and folate; iron studies, LDH and bilirubin; kidney function; TSH and HbA1c; all drawn before the first injection
  • Hematology consultation to confirm the cause and advise on treatment, endoscopy and follow-up
  • Treatment started at intake without waiting for the cause, because of neurological signs: cyanocobalamin 1,000 micrograms into the muscle every other day for seven doses; no folic acid alone; no transfusion while he is stable at rest
  • Maintenance: weekly injections, taught for self-injection, until neurological improvement levels off, then monthly injections for life; high-dose oral cyanocobalamin (at least 1 mg a day) offered as an alternative; vitamin B12 levels not rechecked routinely once treated
  • Response and safety checks: reticulocytes and potassium in the first week, blood count at about five and eight weeks, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine and iron studies at eight weeks, and symptoms at every visit
  • Stomach: upper endoscopy with biopsies by the updated Sydney protocol to confirm autoimmune gastritis and look for neuroendocrine tumors and dysplasia, with a screening colonoscopy at the same session; surveillance interval set from the findings by shared decision; thyroid antibodies checked
  • Nerves and falls: neurological examination (vibration, joint position, reflexes, Romberg, gait, cognition) at each visit; physical therapy for balance and gait; night lights and a clear path at home; a stick outdoors and care on ice
  • Feet: daily skin checks with a mirror, extra-depth shoes with toe fillers and a forefoot rocker sole, no new boots without a fitting, nail and callus care by podiatry every three months, and same-day care for any blister, redness or wound
  • Mood and cognition: PHQ-9 and MoCA at intake and after treatment, since vitamin B12 deficiency can affect both

resource.title: Robert Peary synthetic care plan
resource.description: Pernicious anemia in an older man with old frostbite amputations: a 62-year-old retired naval officer and polar explorer comes in with four months of fatigue, breathlessness, pallor, a sore tongue and numb, unsteady feet. The episode covers the blood count, MCV, smear and reticulocytes; vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine and folate; iron studies; intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies and gastrin; treatment without delay when nerves are affected, with intramuscular cyanocobalamin loading, a weekly phase and lifelong monthly maintenance under the 1907 British Society for Haematology guideline and the 1917 NICE guideline, and high-dose oral therapy as an alternative; the reticulocyte response and the risk of low potassium early in treatment; restrictive transfusion; upper endoscopy for neuroendocrine tumors and gastric cancer risk and its surveillance under the 1914 AGA clinical practice update on atrophic gastritis; screening for autoimmune thyroid disease and diabetes; iron deficiency unmasked by recovery; the examination of subacute combined degeneration and its partial recovery; neuropathy and falls; and foot care for a man with old toe amputations, with footwear, daily skin checks and podiatry.
